items.basis: The candidate fails to address that nitrification in chloraminated systems is primarily driven by ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB) and nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB) which can adapt to residual disinfectant concentrations, making hydraulic residence time reduction insufficient without addressing the ammonia source that feeds these bacteria.

The candidate violates the boundary condition of maintaining total chlorine residual above 1.0 mg/L at the farthest customer because flushing dead-end mains will inevitably reduce disinfectant contact time throughout the system, potentially dropping below the required threshold at the farthest customer points.

The evidence [doi:10.1038/s41522-020-00144-w] shows that residual chlorine has complex, non-linear effects on biofilms and can actually promote certain bacterial communities under certain conditions, contradicting the simplistic assumption that reducing HRT alone will consistently reduce nitrite.

The candidate cannot beat the baseline because the flushing program is essentially a maintenance activity already implemented by many utilities during routine operations, offering no fundamental improvement over standard distribution system management practices.

The program cannot be implemented as claimed because the required flushing frequency to maintain HRT < 48 hours in all dead-end mains would require prohibitively high water volumes and create hydraulic disturbances that would compromise water quality across the entire distribution network.

The prediction fails to pin down critical variables including the actual biofilm density and composition in each dead-end main, the variable chlorine demand throughout the system, and the impact of pipe material on disinfectant decay rates, making the 50% nitrite reduction claim untestable and unverifiable.
